'''''Turnera ulmifolia''''', commonly known as the '''ramgoat dashalong'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TUUL|taxon=Turnera ulmifolia|access-date=12 December 2015}}</ref>, '''yellow alder''', '''Cuban buttercup''' or '''West Indian holly''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Passifloraceae]]. It is native to [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], the [[Caribbean]], and parts of northern [[South America]] and southern [[Florida]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:836702-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref> The plant is widely cultivated as an ornamental in tropical and subtropical regions and has become naturalized in many parts of the world.<ref>{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia (yellow alder) |url=https://plantpono.org/high-risk-plants/turnera-ulmifolia-yellow-alder/ |website=Plant Pono |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref>
The species is sometimes confused with the closely related ''[[Turnera diffusa]]'' (damiana), leading to misidentification in horticultural and herbal trade.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Joshi|first1=V.C.|last2=Rao|first2=A.S.|last3=Wang|first3=Y.H.|last4=Avula|first4=B.|last5=Khan|first5=I.A.|title=Taxonomic clarification on Turnera diffusa Ward and its demarcation from “false damiana” using fluorescence, scanning electron microscopy, HPTLC and UPLC|journal=Planta Medica|date=2009|volume=75|issue=4|doi=10.1055/s-2009-1216454}}</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Ramgoat dashalong or yellow alder.jpg|thumb|Immature yellow flower]]

''Turnera ulmifolia'' is a perennial subshrub or small shrub that typically grows 0.5–1.5 m tall. The stems are erect and become woody at the base with age.<ref>{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia |url=https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Turnera+ulmifolia |website=Useful Tropical Plants |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref>
The leaves are alternate, elliptic to lanceolate, and usually 2–10 cm long, with serrated margins and a slightly rough surface.<ref name="tropicalplants">{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia |url=https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Turnera+ulmifolia |website=Useful Tropical Plants |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref> The plant produces solitary bright yellow flowers in the leaf axils. Each flower has five petals and five sepals, with numerous stamens surrounding the central pistil.
The flowers are short-lived: they typically open early in the morning around sunrise and wilt or close by midday, lasting only a few hours.<ref>{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia (yellow alder) |url=https://plantpono.org/high-risk-plants/turnera-ulmifolia-yellow-alder/ |website=Plant Pono |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref>
The fruit is a small capsule containing several seeds which are released when the capsule splits open at maturity.<ref name="tropicalplants" />

== Taxonomy ==
The species was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753 in ''[[Species Plantarum]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Linnaeus |first=Carl |title=Species Plantarum |year=1753 |page=271}}</ref>
Historically the genus ''Turnera'' was placed in the family [[Turneraceae]], but molecular phylogenetic studies led to the group being incorporated into the family [[Passifloraceae]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=APG III |title=An update of the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group classification for the orders and families of flowering plants |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |year=2009 |volume=161 |pages=105–121}}</ref>
The specific epithet ''ulmifolia'' means “elm-leaved,” referring to the serrated leaf margins resembling those of species in the genus ''Ulmus''.

== Distribution and habitat ==
The native range of ''Turnera ulmifolia'' extends from Mexico and Central America through the Caribbean to northern South America and southern Florida.<ref>{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:836702-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref>
The species commonly grows in open, sunny habitats including roadsides, coastal scrub, disturbed areas, grasslands, and forest clearings.<ref name="tropicalplants" /> It tolerates poor soils and drought conditions and can grow in cracks of pavement, walls, and rocky substrates.
Due to its ornamental use, it has been introduced and naturalized in tropical regions worldwide, including parts of Africa, Asia, and the Pacific islands.<ref>{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia (yellow alder) invasive profile |url=https://plantpono.org/high-risk-plants/turnera-ulmifolia-yellow-alder/ |website=Plant Pono |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
The flowers provide nectar for a variety of pollinators including bees and butterflies. The plant is capable of self-pollination but also benefits from insect pollination.<ref>{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia (yellow alder) |url=https://plantpono.org/high-risk-plants/turnera-ulmifolia-yellow-alder/ |website=Plant Pono |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref>
Larvae of certain butterflies, including the tawny coster (''Acraea terpsicore''), feed on the leaves.<ref>{{cite web |title=Acraea terpsicore host plants |url=https://www.ifoundbutterflies.org |website=Butterflies of India |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref>
Seeds may be dispersed by ants and other insects that collect and transport them from fallen fruits, aiding the plant’s spread in suitable habitats.

== Cultivation ==
''Turnera ulmifolia'' is widely cultivated as an ornamental shrub due to its bright yellow flowers, drought tolerance, and ability to bloom for long periods in warm climates.<ref name="tropicalplants" />
It grows best in full sun and well-drained soils and is easily propagated by seeds or cuttings.
Because it readily self-seeds and tolerates disturbed environments, it can escape cultivation and become naturalized.

== Invasive status ==
In some regions outside its native range, including several Pacific islands and tropical parts of Asia, ''Turnera ulmifolia'' is considered an invasive or potentially invasive species.<ref>{{cite web |title=Turnera ulmifolia (yellow alder) invasive plant |url=https://plantpono.org/high-risk-plants/turnera-ulmifolia-yellow-alder/ |website=Plant Pono |access-date=8 March 2026}}</ref>
Its rapid reproduction, tolerance of poor soils, and ability to form dense stands allow it to compete with native vegetation in disturbed habitats.

== Phytochemistry ==
Phytochemical studies of ''Turnera ulmifolia'' have identified several classes of compounds including flavonoids, alkaloids, tannins, and other phenolic compounds.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Phytochemical investigation of Turnera ulmifolia |journal=Journal of Medicinal Plants Research |year=2011}}</ref>
These compounds are thought to contribute to the plant's reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

== Traditional medicine ==
The plant has been used in traditional medicine in parts of South America and the Caribbean. In Brazil it is known as ''chanana'', and infusions made from the leaves are used in folk medicine to treat gastrointestinal disorders and ulcers.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Effects of tea from Turnera ulmifolia on mouse gastric mucosa support the Turneraceae as a new source of antiulcerogenic drugs |journal=Biological & Pharmaceutical Bulletin |year=2002 |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=487–491}}</ref>
Experimental studies have shown that extracts of the plant may reduce gastric lesions in animal models.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Effects of tea from Turnera ulmifolia on mouse gastric mucosa support the Turneraceae as a new source of antiulcerogenic drugs |journal=Biological & Pharmaceutical Bulletin |year=2002 |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=487–491}}</ref>
Other reported traditional uses include treatment of inflammation, coughs, and respiratory conditions.
